For those out of the loop, Github recently threatened to remove a code repository for using the word retard (Original Voat thread). Among other episodes (such as this one), it's clear that Github is taking a more active role on their content.

Many people are saying that Github has the right to censor its content. Perhaps Github is legally allowed to do so, but does that make it justified? Github is a major part in the open source software community as the de facto version control software, and their censorship (in my opinion) sets a dangerous precedent. And simply migrating to an alternative may not be as straight-forward as it may seem.

What are your guys' opinions on this? Personally I am disappointed that Github would meddle in something so trivial. It sets a bad precedent for arbitrary judgment, and I don't think the argument that the freedom of speech needn't apply to commercial entities justifies censorship.
Github's Censorship Attempts: Are They Justified Because They're a Private Entity?

Perhaps Github is legally allowed to do so, but does that make it justified?

This is really the crux of the issue. Github's operators are legally allowed to censor and police their own service. Are their actions justifiable? Do they make sense? Are they morally correct? That's all a matter of opinion and depends entirely on who you ask, but ultimately it just doesn't matter.

Personally I find the idea of services like Github (or any online service) trying to play "tone police" with user-made content to be a completely unnecessary overreach, and a move that goes against the the spirit of the site.

One thing to consider is Github is used by professionals. There is a point where they have an incentive to maintain a tone that is appropriate for professionals to use the site. While we in this subverse are generally anti-censorship, there's a point where we reasonably say that an employer can keep us from saying "nigger" over and over again. Likewise, employers would want the sites their employees use to have similar guidelines to the actual workplace. Reasonably, the market would develop to have an unrestricted site and a site with a professional tone. There's no reason in my mind that a site should be criticized for being the latter, as they fill a need that has a purpose to exist.

By definition, professionals get paid for what they do. I think you overstep the mark if you assert the majority of github users are getting paid. Those projects with paid contributors and business sponsors are free to establish their own codes of conduct and moderate their github repository accordingly. Enforcing a "professional" code of conduct on every project is unwarranted, not to mention an unnecessary expense for github. Projects should be self-governing.

Personally, before incorporating a github project into my commercial offering, I would want to know and seriously reconsider if the devs engaged in such sophomoric name calling.
